item.title: Why operational excellence will define the next phase of India’s startup growth
item.description: Startups often prioritise funding, sales and expansion while overlooking the operational foundations needed to sustain growth. The article explores why strong processes, reliable data and governance are essential to building scalable businesses.
item.content:encoded:
Growth rarely announces itself. It arrives as a signed term sheet on a Friday evening, a large client wanting to go live in three weeks, or an investor doubling a commitment.

But the win is rarely the hard part. The hard part is the Monday after.

That Monday tells you whether you have built a company or simply had a good quarter.

When operations become a competitive advantage

In most startups, operations sit in the back seat. It is the team that asks for approvals, slows down contracts, and says “not yet” when sales say “yes”. Founders tolerate it the way one tolerates a seatbelt.

I have never accepted that framing. Bain & Company’s long-running research on growth found that 85% of the barriers to profitable growth are internal, with revenue outgrowing talent at the top of the list. Companies rarely lose to the market. They lose to their own machinery, and that machinery is operations.

Build it before you need it

Early on, operations feel optional. A small team, a founder who knows everything, a spreadsheet that works. Why design controls for a business that fits in one room?

Because by the time you feel the need, you are already late. Operations built in the middle of a growth spurt is built under pressure: rushed hires, patched processes, controls bolted on after something breaks. Worse, it takes bandwidth from growth itself. The team that should be closing the next client is busy repairing the last one. You slow down precisely when you meant to accelerate.

Nobody lays the tracks after the train has left the station.

This is not a case for bloat. It is a case for sequencing. Build the backbone one stage ahead of where you are, lean and proportionate, so the organisation absorbs growth instead of buckling under it.

The companies that scale most smoothly are rarely the ones scrambling when growth arrives; the reporting, controls and people for the next stage are already in place. Investors notice the difference.

In due diligence, a clean data room and a well-documented control environment often say more about a company's readiness than its growth curve does.

Run on data, not opinions

Operations is also where a company's data lives, or should. Every onboarding, approval, and report generates information. Most startups treat it as exhaust. The better ones treat it as instrumentation. When operations own clean, consistent data, leadership stops arguing about whose number is right and starts debating what to do about it. You see a bottleneck forming before a client complains. And automation and AI, which nearly every board is now asking about, only work on data you can trust.

Automate a messy process and you simply get the mess faster.

If your founders and your operations team are looking at different numbers, you do not have a data problem. You have an operations problem.

Never pay for the same lesson twice

The same discipline applies to mistakes. A mistake made once is a lesson; made twice, it is a choice.

Every error in a growing firm should leave something behind, whether a changed control, a clearer owner, or a better checklist.

The corollary matters as much. If the same method keeps producing the same disappointing result, the problem is rarely effort. It is the method. Operations should be the function that notices, asks why, and has the licence to change how the work gets done. Processes are not scripture. They are hypotheses, and good operators keep testing them.

Bring operations in before growth is sold, not after

For founders and boards redrawing their organisation charts this year, one test is telling. Do operations hear about a new product, market, or client after it is sold, or while it is being designed? If it is after, operations will always be firefighting, and firefighters rarely get to build anything.

Put operations where growth is planned, not at the end of the line where growth is processed. Give it a seat in strategy reviews, a voice in pricing and launches, and a mandate to say "here is how", not just "not yet".

Three questions are worth asking every quarter:

● If our business doubled next quarter, what would break first?

● Which decisions still need the founder, and should they?

● Would our records survive an investor's due diligence this week?

Will your growth last, or was it just a good quarter?

There is an old military line: amateurs talk strategy, professionals talk logistics.

India's startup story so far has been told in the language of strategy: rounds, valuations, category creation. The next chapter will be about sustaining growth rather than merely achieving it, and it will be told in the language of execution and governance. Momentary growth is an event. Sustained growth is a capability. And capability, in the end, is what operations builds.

(Sandesha Jaitapkar is the COO at Artha Group)

item.title: Aina launches Rs 47,000 ring to bring AI agents to your fingertips
item.description: Aina AI ring launches at Rs 47,000, with AI agents, voice commands and gesture controls. The Bengaluru startup offers an early-bird price of Rs 37,700.
item.content:encoded:
What if booking a cab, sending a message or managing a meeting required nothing more than a flick of your thumb? Bengaluru- and San Francisco-based startup startup Aina believes the next phase of artificial intelligence will be less about asking machines questions and more about letting them anticipate what people need. At a private launch event in Bengaluru, the startup unveiled an AI-powered smart ring that combines a colour display, voice commands and gesture-based controls. Priced at $499 (Rs 47,000), the device is available for pre-order at a limited early-bird price starting at $399 (Rs 37,700), with shipments expected to begin in January 2027. Unlike conventional smart rings, which largely focus on health and fitness tracking, Aina wants its device to become an everyday interface between users and AI agents. The premise is simple: AI agents are getting smarter, but using them still involves unlocking phones, navigating apps and approving individual actions. Aina wants to reduce that friction. Its proposition revolves around a question displayed during the launch presentation: What if AI didn't wait to be asked?

An AI ring that anticipates your next move

To simplify these interactions, Aina has built its ring around three features: Cues, Voice and Remote.

Cues uses contextual information, including routines and connected applications, to anticipate what users might want to do next. For instance, if someone regularly books a cab around the same time each morning, the ring could suggest booking a ride without waiting for an explicit request. At the launch event, Aina demonstrated a ride-booking interaction that illustrated how everyday transactions could be completed through minimal gestures.

The ring can be operated using a five-way joystick-like control, allowing users to approve or reject suggestions with their thumb without reaching for a smartphone. Aina says its context-aware intelligence can learn users' routines and anticipate relevant actions over the next 15 minutes, drawing on information from the iPhone, Mac and connected services. The company showcased integrations involving Uber, Apple Music, Spotify, phone calls, calendar meetings, smart home controls and email actions.

The second interaction method, Voice, allows users to dictate notes, set reminders, send messages and issue commands. Aina also showcased use cases involving WhatsApp and Telegram, alongside Mac dictation through Wispr Flow. The third feature, Remote, turns the ring into a controller for connected devices. According to the company, users can manage music, phone calls, smart home appliances and meeting controls without picking up another device.

What goes into the $499 ring?

According to specifications presented at the Bengaluru launch, the ring weighs less than 13 grams and features a titanium body, full-colour display, haptic feedback and directional audio. The company claims up to 18 hours of battery life and plans to offer the device in four colours: Eclipse Black, Amber Gold, Mercury Silver and Slate Titanium, across seven sizes. Aina also highlighted a five-way control mechanism called the Shifter, which works alongside its gesture-based interface.

The startup says the ring will come with an open developer platform, allowing third-party developers to build new interactions and integrations. It also showcased support for AI agent platforms including Muse, Grokbot and Instinct. The company currently supports iOS and Mac, with further integrations expected to be announced later. Whether its open platform translates into a substantial developer ecosystem will become clearer once the device reaches customers.

From Ultrahuman to Aina

Aina was founded by Apoorv Shankar, who previously served as vice-president of hardware at Bengaluru-based wearable technology company Ultrahuman. Shankar founded Aina in May 2025 as a human-computer interaction lab, focusing on how people could interact with intelligent software beyond conventional screens and keyboards. The startup raised $5.5 million in seed funding in July 2026, as previously reported by YourStory. The round was led by Redstart Labs and 360 ONE Asset, with participation from MIXI Global Investments, Antler, Blume Founders Fund and angel investors including CRED founder Kunal Shah and Razorpay co-founders Harshil Mathur and Shashank Kumar. The funding was earmarked for commercialising its AI-first hardware interface and expanding its engineering and product teams.

Aina says it spent around 15 months developing the technology and began testing the ring with a limited group of users in October 2026.

Can a ring replace everyday smartphone interactions?

Aina's launch comes as technology companies experiment with new ways of bringing AI into daily life. While smartphones remain the dominant interface for digital services, the rise of AI agents is prompting startups to rethink how people give instructions, approve actions and receive information. Aina's approach is to make that interface smaller and more contextual, with users retaining control over whether suggested actions are executed.

However, at $499, the ring is a premium purchase, particularly when smartphones and smartwatches already perform many of the functions it promises. Its usefulness will depend on how accurately its AI anticipates user needs, how reliably it works with third-party services and whether the thumb-based controls become intuitive enough for daily use. Battery life, voice recognition and application support will also matter when the product moves beyond controlled demonstrations. For now, Aina's claims remain to be tested at scale, with commercial deliveries planned for January 2027.

item.title: DevSparks 2026 heads to Delhi to explore agentic AI and the future of software development
item.description: YourStory’s flagship developer summit makes its Delhi NCR debut on December 5, bringing together developers, technology leaders, startups, and enterprises for hands-on sessions on AI, cloud infrastructure, cybersecurity, and emerging technologies.
item.content:encoded:
As AI changes how software is developed, tested, and deployed, developers are having to learn new tools and adapt to new ways of working. From autonomous coding agents and multi-agent systems to AI-powered infrastructure and cybersecurity, the technologies shaping software development are evolving rapidly.

Against this backdrop, DevSparks 2026, YourStory’s flagship developer summit, will make its Delhi NCR debut on December 5, bringing together developers, startups, enterprises, and Global Capability Centres (GCCs) for a day of technical deep dives, hands-on sessions, and discussions on the future of software development.

Following editions in Pune, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Chennai, the Delhi event will be held at Crowne Plaza, Gurugram. More than 500 developers are expected to attend, with over 15 technology leaders taking the stage and more than 10 deep-dive sessions planned.

Across its four previous editions, DevSparks has brought together more than 27,000 developers, 173 speakers, and 50 partners.

DevSparks 2026 is a nationwide initiative aimed at equipping India's developer community with skills in coding agents, agentic AI, multi-agent orchestrators, AI SDKs, and GenAI tools that can improve productivity. Delhi NCR's strong developer community, startup ecosystem, and growing enterprise and GCC presence make it the natural next stop for the summit.

Delhi NCR's growing technology ecosystem

Delhi NCR is already one of India's leading startup hubs. According to Tracxn’s Delhi NCR Tech Annual Funding Report 2025, tech companies in the region raised $2.9 billion in 2025, with autotech leading the way with $1.4 billion. 

Delhi-based tech firms accounted for 51% of all funding raised by tech companies across the region in 2025. 

It was also a big year for exits: 19 companies went public, including Lenskart, Physics Wallah, and Pine Labs, while Delhivery bought Ecom Express for $165 million and Everstone Capital acquired Wingify for $200 million.

The Delhi government is taking steps to further strengthen the ecosystem.

The Delhi Start-up and Incubation Policy 2026, approved in July, provides for Rs 400 crore over five years to support incubation infrastructure, mentorship, and incentives for local entrepreneurs.

In October, the Delhi Cabinet also approved the Go-Delhi Foundation, with an initial outlay of Rs 50 crore. The initiative aims to give startups and MSMEs access to product engineering, prototyping and testing facilities.

The government’s draft IT Policy 2026–2031 proposes setting up more than 200 GCCs and training five to six lakh young people by 2031 in areas such as AI, cloud computing, cybersecurity, and data analytics.

It also proposes a Delhi State Data Centre, expected to become operational by 2027, and AI computing credits among other incentives.

These initiatives could create more opportunities for developers working in AI, cloud infrastructure, and cybersecurity, while strengthening the region’s technology ecosystem.

Agentic AI takes centre stage

Agentic AI is becoming an important area of focus for developers and enterprises, and will be a key part of the DevSparks Delhi agenda.

Sessions will explore how to build autonomous agentic systems and develop multi-agent orchestration for coding, workflows, and business operations.

Developers will also examine real-world applications of multimodal AI, including systems that work with text, code, images, video, and speech in production environments.

Building and scaling AI applications

Beyond agentic AI, the summit will examine what it takes to move AI applications from prototypes to production.

Sessions will cover building applications with AI-first frameworks, integrating AI into sectors such as fintech, healthcare, commerce, manufacturing and agritech, and using Edge AI and the Internet of Things (IoT).

The programme will also look at how AI-driven testing can improve developer productivity.

On the infrastructure side, discussions will cover AI-optimised cloud systems, chips, and accelerators, along with multi-cloud, hybrid, and sovereign cloud models for enterprises.

Other areas of focus include data pipelines, governance, cybersecurity threats, and AI-driven defences.

GCCs, skills, and emerging opportunities

With GCCs an important part of Delhi's technology growth plans, DevSparks will also examine how enterprises and GCCs are preparing their workforces for new technologies.

Sessions will look at trends in upskilling, hiring, and workforce readiness as AI becomes increasingly integrated with other technologies.

The discussions will focus on the skills developers need to remain relevant and the opportunities emerging within India’s leading technology enterprises and GCCs.

A day of learning for developers

DevSparks Delhi will offer developers opportunities to learn through technical deep dives, workshops, masterclasses, and real-world case studies.

The sessions are designed to help participants apply AI to practical problems, explore technological advances beyond AI, and identify new career opportunities.

As AI becomes more widely used in software development and enterprise technology, the summit will focus on the tools, skills, and technical knowledge developers need to build and deploy applications.

DevSparks Delhi 2026 will take place on December 5 at Crowne Plaza, Gurugram. Register now to secure your spot. 

Edited by Teja Lele

item.title: AI-powered cyberattacks put Indian fintechs on alert; Shiprocket turns profitable in Q2 FY27
item.description: An advisory from the government body said the AI-assisted financial threat is still active and warns BFSI entities to treat it as an “immediate and continuing threat”.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader, 

Investor appetite for India’s B2C ecommerce sector appears to be cooling. Funding fell 33% to $1.6 billion across 356 rounds between January and November 3, 2026, compared with $2.4 billion across 621 rounds in the year-ago period, according to Tracxn. Late-stage and seed-stage funding declined 51% and 50%, respectively, while early-stage investments remained relatively stable, growing 3%.

While investors are becoming more cautious, the AI infrastructure boom is facing a different challenge: rising public concerns over its impact on local communities. OpenAI has pledged to pay the full electricity costs of data centres it owns and operates, while committing to greater transparency around construction plans and community consultations. 

Meanwhile, India's cybersecurity watchdog CERT-In has warned of AI-driven attacks targeting fintech firms and NBFCs, with hackers exploiting payment systems to siphon off funds.

Cybersecurity concerns are also surfacing across global financial services. Binance has revoked all API keys linked to third-party trading platform SignalPlus following a potential security issue reported by the company. The exchange said its own systems and user funds remain safe, and advised affected users to review their trading positions before reconnecting. 

The risks extend beyond financial services. A cyberattack targeting refrigeration control systems at three sites operated by France's national blood service raised storage temperatures for plasma and other blood products. Monitoring systems detected the breach in time, allowing staff to move supplies before any products were compromised. Authorities are investigating the incident.  

In today’s newsletter: 

  • CERT-In flags AI-driven attacks on NBFCs, fintech firms
  • Saraniya Periasamy’s journey at Agnikul Cosmos
  • Shiprocket turns profitable in Q2 FY27

Here’s your trivia for today: What is a 'zero-day' vulnerability in cybersecurity? (Scroll down for the answer)

Artificial Intelligence

CERT-In flags AI-driven attacks on NBFCs, fintech firms 

AI-powered cyberattacks targeting India’s financial services sector are escalating, prompting a fresh warning from CERT-In. The government cybersecurity agency has flagged a campaign called CRAFTY FALCON, which uses AI tools to target NBFCs, fintech companies and other financial institutions. The attacks have involved exploiting payment systems and stealing cryptocurrency assets. 

Key takeaways: 

  • CERT-In has identified an active campaign called CRAFTY FALCON, which uses machine intelligence and AI-assisted tools to target financial institutions. 
  • Attackers have exploited merchant settlement APIs to move funds and stolen wallet keys to siphon cryptocurrency assets. 
  • The campaign has affected NBFCs, digital lending platforms, payment aggregators, fintech firms and crypto exchanges, with CERT-In warning that the threat remains active.

Inspiration

Saraniya Periasamy’s journey at Agnikul Cosmos

From joining a space-tech startup with no prior experience in the sector to leading the development of an orbital launch vehicle, Saraniya Periasamy’s journey has been anything but conventional. As Agnikul Cosmos’ fourth employee, she has played a key role in the company’s efforts to build indigenous rocket technology. Today, as Executive Vice President and Vehicle Director, she is helping steer the development of Agnibaan while encouraging more women to explore careers in space-tech. 

Breaking barriers: 

  • Saraniya joined Agnikul Cosmos eight years ago as a Systems Engineer and went on to lead the development of its Agnibaan SOrTeD suborbital mission, which successfully flew in May 2024. 
  • She is now leading the development of Agnibaan, the company's orbital launch vehicle, with plans to demonstrate booster recovery and reuse, alongside exploring ways to repurpose its upper stage. 
  • Having transitioned from civil engineering and ocean technology into space, Saraniya believes self-doubt is often a bigger barrier for women than a lack of opportunities. 

Ecommerce

Shiprocket turns profitable in Q2 FY27

Shiprocket turned profitable in Q2 FY27, reporting a net profit of Rs 60 lakh against a loss of Rs 20.3 crore a year ago, while revenue grew 35% to Rs 673.6 crore. Its emerging business, led by Martech and omnichannel solutions, grew 61% during the quarter. The company also repaid Rs 242 crore in borrowings following its IPO, ending the first half debt-free.

News & updates

  • Ambulance pricing: Blinkit Ambulance will charge Rs 2,500 for non-emergency transfers, while emergency services will continue to remain free. Zomato founder Deepinder Goyal said the move aims to discourage routine hospital visits and transfers from using emergency ambulances, keeping them available for critical cases.

  • Ronaldo retires: Cristiano Ronaldo will retire from Portugal's national team after the November international break, ending a 23-year international career. He leaves as men's international football's record goalscorer with 146 goals in 234 appearances, having led Portugal to the Euro 2016 title and two Nations League victories.

item.title: Blinkit Ambulance to charge Rs 2,500 for non-emergency cases
item.description: Zomato founder Deepinder Goyal noted that a growing share of bookings for its free ambulance service were for routine checkups, hospital visits and hospital-to-home transfers.
item.content:encoded:
Blinkit Ambulance, the free service from the quick commerce company, will now start charging Rs 2,500 for non-emergency transfers.

“Emergency transfers–free, as always. Non-emergency transfers–₹2,500, charged after the trip. Broadly in line with what private ambulances charge. This money goes to the Eternal Foundation, which runs these ambulances and will help us scale them even further,” Zomato founder Deepinder Goyal said in a post on X.

Goyal noted that Blinkit Ambulance was started as a spirit of service, and in the last two years, it has served around 20,000 emergency cases and more than 42,000 cases in total. “We haven't charged a single rupee for any of them. And we want to keep it that way,” he remarked.

The reason for the change is that a growing share of bookings were for routine checkups, hospital visits and hospital-to-home transfers, the post noted. As Goyal remarked that every such booking requires a fully equipped emergency ambulance with paramedics.

I started Zomato with a spirit of service. Blinkit Ambulance is what that spirit of service looks like today.

In the last 2 years, we have served ~20,000 emergency cases (~42,000 cases in total). We haven't charged a single rupee for any of them. And we want to keep it that way.… https://t.co/lHeo9zo3bN

— Deepinder Goyal (@deepigoyal) November 5, 2026

“We hope that this charge will dramatically drop the usage of our Ambulances for non-emergency cases. 10-minute ambulances have saved and can save thousands of lives, and we need to keep them available for emergencies that need them the most,” Goyal said.

He also highlighted the challenge faced in providing free ambulance services is the availability of paramedics. However, he further added that they are planning to introduce Blinkit Ambulance to all major cities in the country in the next 2-4 years.

item.title: Why AI’s biggest challenge lies beneath the model
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Michael Cronin of Couchbase explained why fragmented data infrastructure remains a major barrier to enterprise AI adoption and why companies need to fix their data systems before scaling AI applications.
item.content:encoded:
AI models are becoming increasingly accessible, but turning them into products that work reliably remains a challenge, particularly when enterprises are dealing with fragmented data infrastructure.

At TechSparks 2026, Michael Cronin, Vice President, Sales, Asia-Pacific, Japan & India, Couchbase, joined Shivani Muthanna, Senior Director – Strategic Content & Video, YourStory, for a discussion on moving AI beyond experimentation, production failures, governance challenges, customer experience, and India's growing role in AI innovation.

AI’s missing link: the data layer

Over the decades, large enterprises have adopted different databases and point solutions to address specific problems. While each solved an immediate need, the result has often been a fragmented data layer, with multiple systems that struggle to work together.

Cronin sees this fragmentation as a major barrier to AI adoption. Citing industry estimates, he said 70–80% of AI development projects never reach production, while an MIT study found that 95% fail to become profitable.

Couchbase’s operational data platform is designed to address this challenge by helping enterprises consolidate their data infrastructure.

Rather than trying to fix everything at once, Cronin advised companies to start small.

“My advice to founders and enterprises that are struggling with the fragmentation of the data layer is to pick your most critical use cases first,” he said.

Cronin cited the example of Tesco, the UK retailer with a large global Capability Center (GCC) in Bengaluru. Its multiple systems were affecting customer experience, particularly during busy shopping periods such as Black Friday and weekends.

Tesco began consolidating its data layer, starting with a single instance and use case before extending the effort across its technology stack.

The consolidation enabled the retailer to handle millions of transactions per second with sub-millisecond latency. According to Cronin, the example shows how companies can begin addressing fragmentation through a single use case before expanding the changes across their operations.

AI moves at machine speed. Can data keep up?

The pressure to develop AI products has led many enterprises to prioritize models and applications. However, pilots often run on small datasets in controlled environments, leaving organizations unprepared for the demands of production.

Cronin pointed to the growing scale of machine-generated traffic.

“Eighteen months ahead of schedule, machine traffic has overtaken human traffic on the internet. That’s the AI scale. That’s the machine speed scale that enterprises need to operate on,” he said.

When AI applications encounter real-world workloads, fragmented data systems can prevent them from operating reliably at scale.

The growing use of AI agents adds to the challenge. As agents become more autonomous and take on decision-making responsibilities, enterprises need to ensure they can access the right data while working within appropriate governance frameworks.

Fragmented systems can make communication and governance more difficult, limiting the ability of agents to operate autonomously.

Cronin also urged enterprises to reconsider how they allocate their AI investments. While models are evolving rapidly, enterprise data remains a critical asset.

“The models are rentable. Today’s best model is yesterday's newspaper. The true asset for the enterprise is the data,” he said.

More API layers aren't the answer

As enterprises began recognizing that fragmented data was holding back their AI initiatives, many responded by adding APIs and connectors to link existing systems.

Cronin cautioned that this approach could introduce further complexity rather than solve the underlying problem. Each additional connection brings latency, risk, and another potential point of failure.

Instead, he recommended consolidating the data layer so applications and AI agents can communicate with it more directly, bringing data closer to customers.

According to Cronin, many enterprises, including large GCCs in India, are now reassessing their architecture to address data fragmentation. Without these changes, further investment in AI development could lead to the same problems.

Consolidating data can also improve customer experience by helping systems manage growing demand, remain available and respond quickly.

As customers expect more from AI-powered services, having data available at the edge is becoming increasingly important.

India: From back office to innovation leader

Cronin observed that business cultures vary across the Asia-Pacific region, but fragmented data infrastructure remains a common challenge for AI adoption.

At the same time, India is becoming an important centre for AI innovation and decision-making.

He noted that 80% of Couchbase's top 50 global accounts have a significant presence in India, with much of their AI innovation and leadership based in the country.

Couchbase is also expanding its presence in India, with its Asia-Pacific headquarters moving to Bengaluru. Its Indian enterprise customers include Air India, Airtel, BigBasket, and Mahindra Finance.

According to Cronin, India’s role in global business has moved beyond cost savings, with innovation, leadership, and important business decisions increasingly taking place here.

He cited Air India's next-generation entertainment platform, which is being built on Couchbase. The platform aims to provide passengers with personalized shopping and entertainment experiences even when an aircraft is offline.

For Cronin, the project shows how Indian enterprises are using technology to improve customer experiences under real-world operating conditions.

item.title: How Satin Group’s Sankalp plans to empower India’s next wave of founders
item.description: University incubators play an important role in nurturing early-stage ideas, but Sankalp aims to go further by helping entrepreneurs bridge the gap between developing a concept and preparing it for the market.
item.content:encoded:
India’s startup ecosystem is witnessing a growing wave of innovation in climate action and sustainability. From students developing affordable technology solutions for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) to early-stage entrepreneurs tackling circular economy challenges, the ideas are promising. But turning a climate-focused idea into a scalable business requires more than passion. Founders need access to capital, industry networks and structured mentorship to translate their vision into viable enterprises.

Recognising these gaps, Satin Group, based in Gurugram, Haryana, launched Sankalp this September. It is a platform designed to nurture sustainability-focused ideas from students and early-stage entrepreneurs. In an exclusive interaction with YourStory, Pramod Marar, CEO of Satin FinServ Limited, discussed the thinking behind the initiative, the importance of non-financial support alongside funding, and the role financial institutions can play in scaling climate innovation.     

Sankalp operates through two distinct tracks: student-led business ideas and early-stage startups. The student track encourages college students to develop technology-driven solutions to climate and environmental challenges. The startup track focuses on young businesses working in areas such as clean mobility, circular economy, waste management, and sustainable supply chains. Sankalp winners stand a chance to win Rs 32 lakh, with Rs 10 lakh for students and Rs 22 lakh for startups.

Applications for the first cohort closed on October 4. Sankalp says the response has been encouraging, with more than 17,000 registrations and over 1,000 teams taking part. Student innovators, it adds, showed a notable interest in technology-led solutions for climate challenges.

“We were pleasantly surprised to see a strong focus among students on creating technology-led solutions in the climate space,” Marar said. 

The genesis of Sankalp

Marar brings more than two decades of experience across banking, microfinance, and sustainability-focused entrepreneurship. Having started his own venture early in his career, he experienced firsthand the challenges faced by entrepreneurs seeking initial funding, particularly those from salaried or service-sector families without access to financial backing.

“Startup wasn’t a cool term at that time; it wasn’t even a term that existed. I come from a middle-class service background family. There was a lot of moral support, but there was no financial support. That’s when I realised how difficult it was to access early-stage capital,” Marar recalled.

While founders may have the passion and business acumen to develop an idea, scaling it requires a broader support system. Capital is only one part of the equation; access to expertise, networks and institutional support can be equally important.

“Most startup founders are very passionate about their ideas and have the acumen to scale them. But scaling requires a lot of elements beyond capital. That’s why we started Sankalp — to help build the ecosystem around sustainability and climate innovation,” Marar said.

Satin Group, which was founded in 1990, comprises three non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) focused on microfinance, housing finance, and corporate and SME lending. Its broader ecosystem also includes Satin Growth Alternatives, a debt fund, and Satin Technologies, its technology arm. This combination of financial and technological capabilities provides the group with multiple avenues to support emerging sustainability-focused businesses.

University incubators play an important role in nurturing early-stage ideas, but Sankalp aims to go further by helping entrepreneurs bridge the gap between developing a concept and preparing it for the market.

“I wouldn’t call it a scaled-down version because we actually try to go beyond the conventional model of incubation. We want to understand whether we can support founders through experienced mentorship, both at an individual level and through institutions, as well as through debt and equity,” Marar said.

With applications closed, Sankalp has moved from a wide pool of ideas to a tighter evaluation. KPMG is the programme’s assessment partner. It is independently evaluating every application against a predefined framework, helping with shortlisting and identifying the most promising ventures. Satin says this keeps the selection objective and based only on merit.

Thirty teams have made it to the virtual jury round, where they will present to a panel of practitioners, venture capital (VC) fund managers and lenders. The shortlisted ventures cover climate tech, circular economy, clean energy, sustainable cities, waste management, water management and sustainable agriculture. 

According to Satin, what stood out was not just the range of ideas but the depth applicants showed in their chosen areas. Judges will look at the strength of the idea, innovation, feasibility, scalability and potential for meaningful impact.

Based on the jury’s assessments, select finalists will go on to the in-person Grand Finale, where they will present before a jury and industry leaders for final evaluation and recognition.

The jury rounds are also meant to open doors beyond the prize money. Both the virtual round and the Grand Finale will have representatives from VC funds, incubation centres and institutional investors, who can evaluate the ideas and explore funding possibilities. Satin has also signed formal arrangements with certain incubation centres to offer institutional mentoring to the selected founders. In addition, Satin Growth Alternatives, the group’s Category II alternative investment fund (AIF), will look at the ideas from an investment angle.

Satin is careful about what this means for funding. At this stage, it says, Sankalp is not an announced debt-and-equity programme. Any financing would be considered case by case, depending on the business model, stage of development, funding needs and suitability, with the aim of finding viable opportunities and exploring ways to support their growth.

For Satin, the programme fits in its wider ambition to help build a more sustainable and climate-resilient economy. Financing remains central to its business, the company says, but Sankalp gives it a chance to engage with emerging innovators and understand how climate-focused business models are evolving, along with the opportunities and challenges in the space. It also helps Satin spot solutions that may, over time, match its own financing capabilities. 

The group has already been building towards this. Satin Finserv set up its Sustainable & Emerging Businesses (SEB) vertical in August 2025 to offer financing to sustainability-oriented and emerging enterprises, with a streamlined process and dedicated relationship support. In the last 12 months, it has disbursed loans of roughly Rs 400 crore to businesses focused on sustainability, either as users or providers of sustainability-focused solutions.

Sankalp complements that effort, Satin says, by helping it discover promising entrepreneurs and innovations.

Why Sankalp matters for India’s green transition

India’s transition towards a low-carbon economy will require more than technological breakthroughs. It will also depend on whether promising innovations can secure funding, find customers, and scale sustainably. Financial institutions, established businesses, and entrepreneurs all have a role to play in building this ecosystem.

Sankalp seeks to bring these stakeholders together, combining access to finance with mentorship and industry connections. Its approach reflects the idea that supporting climate innovation should extend beyond funding a promising idea or awarding a one-time prize.

“Rather than just waiting for institutions to put their money on the table, can financial institutions come together to create a platform that helps founders go beyond simply raising capital?” Marar said.

By seeking to connect entrepreneurs with financing, expertise, and potential commercial partners, Sankalp aims to create a longer-term support system for sustainability-focused businesses.""

item.title: India rebased its GDP. It still can’t see the Rs 34.5 lakh crore women do free
item.description: India’s GDP leaves out unpaid care work worth up to 17% of GDP, mostly done by women. Measuring it is key to more women in jobs.
item.content:encoded:
In February 2026, India moved its GDP base year to 2022-23. The National Accounts of India brought in new data sources and reassessed the size of the informal economy. The exercise carried a lesson that policy debates often forget: economic measurement is not fixed. When the statistical system decides an activity deserves to be captured better, the numbers change.

The same quarter, the economy grew 7.8%, keeping India the fastest-growing major economy even through the first full quarter of steep US tariffs and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. The headlines celebrated. But one kind of work counted for nothing in all that arithmetic: the unpaid domestic and care work that makes every other job possible.

The invisible fifth of the economy

GDP has a defined production boundary, and for good reason. A creche worker paid to look after a child is counted as economic activity. A mother or grandmother doing the same job for free is not. The value has not disappeared; only the payment has.

What sits outside that boundary is large. India's Time Use Survey 2024 shows women aged 15 to 59 spend about 201 minutes a day more than men on unpaid household work. A deeper analysis of the unit-level data puts women's unpaid domestic and care work at 343 minutes a day, against 43 for men. Some 93% of women do this work, compared with 44% of men.

A Ministry of Women and Child Development study values this work at up to Rs 34.5 lakh crore, roughly 15–17% of GDP at weighted average wages. Even the Ministry of Statistics' Time Use Survey report concedes that leaving out unpaid services means GDP "underestimates considerably the total income of a nation."

The global answer is not to abandon GDP but to add a satellite account that measures activity beyond the production boundary. India already has the raw material: two national Time Use Surveys, an accepted valuation method, and a statistical system that has just shown it can rebuild its accounts. What is missing is the decision.

From invisible labour to the second shift

Visibility matters because governments allocate money through the numbers they measure.

According to the UNDP, 44.5% of Indian women outside the labour force cite childcare and homemaking as the main reason. Female labour-force participation has climbed from 23.3% in 2017-18 to about 40% in 2025, by the Periodic Labour Force Survey's measure. Yet women's unpaid workload has barely moved in five years.

A woman who takes a paid job while carrying the same load at home has not been freed to work. She has taken on a second shift. The real policy question is not how to persuade more women to work. It is what infrastructure would make paid work compatible with care.

India's jobs ambition has a care problem

The contradiction shows up in the government's own documents. The Economic Survey's employment chapter calls the care economy a promising source of jobs, and the Economic Survey 2025-26 targets a 55% female workforce. Yet under the Palna scheme, only 11,395 anganwadi-cum-creches had been approved against a target of 17,000 by March 2025. Fewer than 10% of anganwadi centres are in cities, where women's participation is lowest.

The shortfall does not mean the scheme has failed. It means care infrastructure is still being built while the country sets big employment goals. If policymakers want a real rise in women's paid work, childcare must stop being a side programme and become labour-market policy.

What other countries did differently

By the ILO's harmonised estimates, India's female labour-force participation was 32% in 2025. The figure is lower than the PLFS number because the ILO uses a different, internationally comparable definition.

Female labour-force participation, 2025 (ILO estimates)
Country Participation rate
China 59%
Japan 56.5%
Bangladesh 46.5%
India 32%

Source: International Labour Organization (ILO)

Among women of prime working age, participation reaches 85% in Japan and 78% in the United States.

These gaps are policy outcomes, not accidents. Japan raised fathers' take-up of parental leave from 17.1% to 30.1% in a single year by paying for it. Bangladesh, with a fraction of India's output, lifted net pre-primary enrolment from 19.7% in 2018 to 28.5% in 2023 as part of a deliberate push to get women into work. The United States learnt the opposite lesson: prime-age women hit record participation, then gains among mothers of young children stalled where affordable childcare ran out.

No country has gone from developing to developed while leaving half its working-age women outside the paid economy. The road to Viksit Bharat has to take her along, or it will not arrive.

Three ordinary acts of statecraft

1. Measure it. Complete and regularly publish a satellite account for unpaid care work, linked to the Time Use Survey. It should show the work's value, who does it, where it is concentrated and how it changes. The aim is not to inflate GDP but to give planners a second dashboard to act on.

2. Invest in it. The UNDP estimates that spending about 2% of GDP on care services could create more than 11 million jobs. As India urbanises, fertility falls and joint families thin out, who provides care is becoming an economic question, not just a household one.

3. Reclassify it. Care spending should be judged not only as welfare but by its effect on employment, labour supply and productivity. If a childcare centre lets twenty parents stay in work, its value cannot be measured only by the children it serves.

Seeing what GDP cannot

This argument is no longer confined to feminist economics. A working paper from the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister this year calls for moving care "from private burden to social and economic infrastructure." The diagnosis is in, and the evidence backs it. The harder question is whether measurement, budgeting and delivery will follow.

The 2026 rebasing showed that India's statistical system can question long-held assumptions. The same willingness should now extend to the work that sustains the economy from outside its markets.

That means collecting real-time data, publishing a satellite account for unpaid care linked to the Time Use Survey, and treating care infrastructure as a measurable public investment. Every new creche, eldercare service and community care programme should be judged not only by the people it serves but by the paid work it makes possible.

If India wants more women in its workforce, it must budget for the care that makes their work possible. India has shown it can re-measure its economy. Now it must build the care that lets more women take part in it.

item.title: How Pine Labs is building for the agent economy: CTO Sanjeev Kumar on trust, control and execution
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Pine Labs Chief Technology Officer, Sanjeev Kumar showcased how developers, merchants, and teams can put AI agents to work, backed by controls that keep them accountable.
item.content:encoded:
AI agents are starting to run real parts of a business, from finding customers to processing complaints. For banks, fintech companies, and enterprises, that raises a basic question: how far can an agent be trusted to act on its own?

Pine Labs is addressing this question by building an ecosystem that enables AI agents to take on tasks across commerce while keeping their actions accountable. Speaking at its product showcase at TechSparks 2026, Sanjeev Kumar, CTO, Pine Labs, said, “We have tried to make AI a first-class citizen in our ecosystem.”

Over the past 18 months, Pine Labs has been building a commerce operating system around AI agents, combining tools to manage their permissions and track their actions with applications for merchants and enterprise teams. Its Agent Store will open the ecosystem to third-party developers building for merchants and banks.

Building trust into AI agents

For agents to operate in banking and enterprise environments, organizations need to know what they are authorized to do and how their actions can be audited. Pine Labs has developed Grantex, which Kumar described as ‘Open Authorization 2.0 for AI agents’. It assigns each agent a defined set of permissions, an expiry, and a record of the human who authorized it. If an agent authorized to read and draft emails attempts to send one, the action can be blocked and its permissions revoked, including those of any child agents. A tamper-proof, hash-chain audit trail records its actions.

Kumar outlined the work involved in connecting tools and systems, setting up retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), running continuous evaluations, and deciding where human intervention is necessary. These components need to work together before an agent can reliably handle tasks in an enterprise environment.

Pine Labs first deployed the technology across its compliance, finance, HR, and marketing teams, with processing taking place within its own environment. The company is also implementing it with banks in India and overseas.

From cyber fraud complaints to faster resolution

Cora, Pine Labs’ compliance and resolution agent, takes cyber fraud complaints from intake to closure. It matches complaints to transactions, categorizes them, routes them to relevant teams, and prepares responses for review. Kumar said Pine Labs has been able to close some complaints on the same day, compared with the typical three-to-five-day turnaround.

The agent records a 15-step trace of its work, including validation, transaction lookups, settlement checks, and team notifications, along with supporting evidence and confidence levels. When a system connector is unavailable, Cora can use robotic process automation (RPA). In the demonstration, it accessed the government cyber police portal and filled in an action-taken form with transaction details and the disputed amount. A human operator retains control of the password and one-time code and reviews the form before submission.

Opening the platform to developers

Having deployed agents across its own compliance, finance, HR and marketing teams, Pine Labs has since opened its platform to developers and merchant partners. The company is also working with banks in India and overseas.

To show how the technology could be applied beyond its own operations, Kumar pointed to a hackathon organized by Pine Labs and The Ken , which drew more than 380 agent submissions from students, fresh graduates, and engineers across India. The winning entry helped people decide what to cook for dinner.

Developers can create skill files, connect tools, and define tasks in plain English, while AgenticOrg provides visibility into agents, confidence scores, and audit trails via Grantex. The AgenticOrg is intended to help third-party developers build applications for merchants and banks using Pine Labs’ infrastructure.

Helping small merchants run ad campaigns

For smaller businesses, Pine Labs has also developed an ads agent accessible through its merchant interface. Merchants connect their Google Ads account, enter details about their business, and provide a brief, budget, and campaign goal. The agent researches local demand and nearby competitors, then generates ad copy for search, display, and YouTube.

Merchants can request changes and approve the campaign before it goes live. The demonstration showed setup taking about two minutes, with campaign performance and lead routing available through the same interface.

Building an ecosystem for commerce

From internal enterprise workflows and cyber fraud resolution to advertising for small businesses, Pine Labs is applying its agent infrastructure to different parts of commerce. Grantex sets guardrails for what agents can do; AgenticOrg helps teams, individuals, and AI enthusiasts build agents, manage work, and execute tasks, and AgenticOrg is intended to let developers build further applications for merchants and banks.

Pine Labs is betting that the future of commerce will be shaped not just by what AI agents can do, but by how reliably they can do it. By combining the infrastructure to govern agents with applications that solve real business problems, the company is looking to make autonomous AI a working part of commerce, for enterprises, banks, and merchants alike.

item.title: PhysicsWallah, Lenskart, Nykaa post stellar profits
item.description: PhysicsWallah posted a record quarterly top-line and doubled its net profit in Q2FY27. Lenskart’s net profit too rose over two-fold year on year. Nykaa’s profit grew three times, and revenue rose 28% YoY.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader, 

The earnings season is in full swing. 

PhysicsWallah, Lenskart and Nykaa were among the major Indian companies that reported their Q2FY27 results yesterday. 

Expanding scale and cost efficiencies helped PhysicsWallah post a record quarterly top-line and double its net profit. Lenskart’s net profit too rose over two-fold year on year. 

Nykaa’s profit grew three times to Rs 101 crore and revenue rose 28% YoY to Rs 3,006 crore. The beauty and fashion retailer has also acquired an 82% stake in cosmetics brand Simply Nam. The acquisition is expected to help Nykaa expand its premium makeup portfolio.

Meanwhile, Nasdaq-listed SaaS company Freshworks posted a net profit of $18.3 million in the third quarter of 2026, compared with a loss of $4.7 million in the year-ago period. Revenue rose 14% year on year to $245.4 million. 

In an important step towards Atmanirbhar Bharat, the Cabinet has approved a Rs 2,814-crore scheme to promote processing of critical minerals such as lithium and nickel and reduce import dependence. 

In other news, Razorpay has secured Sebi’s approval for its proposed IPO of Rs 5,000-6,000 crore, according to sources. The fintech firm is targeting a valuation of around $5 billion through the public offering. 

Lastly, the Democrats have taken control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives in the US midterm elections, with Indian Americans also making a mark. 

In today’s newsletter: 

  • Lenskart’s profit doubles, revenue grows 36% in Q2
  • PhysicsWallah posts Rs 1,242 Cr top-line; net profit doubles

Here’s your trivia for today: What was the first item ever sold on eBay? (Scroll down for the answer)

Retail

Lenskart’s profit doubles, revenue grows 36% in Q2

Omnichannel eyewear retailer Lenskart’s net profit more than doubled in the second quarter of FY27, while revenue rose 36% year on year. The growth was driven by higher eyewear volumes, premiumisation of products, and stronger demand in India and overseas.

The company reported a net profit of Rs 227 crore in Q2FY27 compared to Rs 102 crore in the year-ago period, a growth of 123%. Revenue was Rs 2,845 crore, a YoY growth of 36%.

Key takeaways: 

  • India revenue grew 35.3% year on year to Rs 1,668 crore, supported by a 26.5% growth in eyewear volumes and rising demand for premium lenses. Same-store sales growth reached 20.8%, compared with 14.8% a year ago. International revenue grew by 29.5%.
  • The company added 143 stores in India, including 94 in Tier II+ markets. It also entered 61 new cities. Its India network now spans 2,868 stores across 665 cities. 
  • Lenskart maintained its consolidated product margin at 70%, compared with 69.2% a year ago, despite continued rupee depreciation. In-house frame manufacturing grew 71.7% YoY, while lens manufacturing increased 52.2%, helping offset currency pressures and strengthen control over product quality and costs.

Edtech

PhysicsWallah posts Rs 1,242 Cr top-line; net profit doubles

The second quarter of the 2027 financial year marked a pivotal turn for PhysicsWallah, as expanding scale and cost efficiencies together yielded a record quarterly top-line and a two-fold growth in net profit. The edtech firm achieved its highest-ever quarterly revenue, driven by expanding student enrolments and enhanced course realisations. 

Key takeaways:  

  • Consolidated revenue from operations reached Rs 1,242.26 crore, up 18.2% YoY. Total income, which includes other non-operating receipts, grew 21.5% YoY to Rs 1,334.64 crore. 
  • Consolidated profit after tax doubled to Rs 142.29 crore in the second quarter, rising 104.1% YoY from Rs 69.72 crore. The net profit in Q2FY27 comes after a loss of Rs 87.04 crore in Q1FY27.
  • “We delivered record revenue and a sharp improvement in profitability, while our learner base kept widening across K-12, vernacular and new categories. Our focus remains on scaling affordable, tech-led education with disciplined capital allocation,” said Founder and Chief Executive Officer Alakh Pandey.

News & updates

  • Startup momentum: Indian startups with a valuation of over $500 million rose to 51 in 2026, from 47 in 2025, despite a lower number of AI companies. Their combined value is about Rs 3.3 lakh crore, with an average valuation of Rs 6,400 crore, according to the 2026 ASK Private Wealth Hurun India Gazelle Index report.  
  • Canva restructuring: Graphic design platform Canva is undertaking a major workforce restructuring affecting 1,271 employees, or 22% of its workforce, as it adapts to rapid technological change. In a note to employees, CEO Melanie Perkins described this as the hardest moment in Canva’s 13-year history. 
  • Accounts hack: Nearly 30 Indian investors who trade US shares through Stockal Securities have reported unauthorised access to their accounts, alleging that their blue-chip holdings, worth millions of dollars in total, were sold off without their consent and replaced with shares in a little-known company that subsequently lost almost 60% of its value.

item.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 05, 2026)
item.description: YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Thursday, November 05, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
From how KumaonKhand, a social enterprise building a hemp-based ecosystem in Uttarakhand, began as a college project and became a full-time venture in 202, to how PhysicsWallah and Lenskart's doubled their profit in the second quarter of FY27, here are the latest developments across sectors.

Featured Stories

How KumaonKhand is building a hemp ecosystem in Uttarakhand

KumaonKhand, a social enterprise building a hemp-based ecosystem in Uttarakhand, began as a college project and became a full-time venture in 2021 with his mother, Sangeeta and Anuj Sharma, the founder and CEO of Alsisar Impact, a social impact incubator and investment firm.

A problem-mapping exercise through an environmental and social lens pointed toward hemp as a solution.

Read more

Latest News

altM raises $10.3M in Series A funding

Specialty chemicals startup altM has raised $10.3 million in a Series A funding round, with Rainmatter by Zerodha and Mela Ventures joining as new investors. Existing backers Omnivore, Theia Ventures, Aureolis Ventures and Spectrum Impact also participated in the round, along with strategic angel investors.

The Bengaluru-based company said it will use the funds to expand its manufacturing capacity, strengthen research and development, support customer qualification programmes, and grow its engineering and commercial teams. The investment will help altM transition from pilot-scale production to commercial manufacturing.

Read more

Funding News

Venomics AI raises $2.7M pre-seed round led by Speciale Invest, South Park Commons

Bengaluru-based Venomics AI, a biotechnology startup spun out of the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), has raised $2.7 million in a pre-seed funding round co-led by Speciale Invest and South Park Commons, with participation from Operators Studio. Co-founded by Kartik Sunagar and Vinay Prabhu, the company uses artificial intelligence, venom biology and laboratory screening to identify venom-derived molecules with therapeutic potential.

The funding will be used to expand its Venom Atlas molecular dataset, strengthen AI and experimental screening capabilities, hire across research and computational science, and validate promising molecules. The startup aims to build a drug discovery platform for global markets.

Other News

Zoho launches restaurant POS platform in India

Zoho has launched a point-of-sale (POS) platform for restaurants in India, with Kolkata-based sweet shop Asha Sweets becoming its first customer. The product is being offered free of charge to restaurants with annual billing of up to Rs 12 lakh, as part of Zoho’s push to bring smaller food businesses onto digital platforms.

In a post on X, Zoho co-founder Sridhar Vembu said Asha Sweets began using Zoho POS for Restaurants during the festive rush. Zoho’s team visited the outlet to observe how the platform was being used during one of its busiest periods.

Read more

Prodigi Connect partners with Indonesia's Lokanima to develop AI-powered animation for Fun Cican

Dubai-headquartered AI video production company Prodigi Connect has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Lokanima, a creative venture of Indonesia's Singhasari Special Economic Zone, to develop animated content based on Indonesian children's entertainment property Fun Cican. 

The partnership will combine Prodigi Connect's AI-native production capabilities and India-based operations with Lokanima's intellectual property access, local creative direction and Indonesian production talent. Prodigi Connect has already produced an approximately one-minute animation sequence as an initial demonstration. The collaboration aims to reduce the cost and time associated with conventional animation production while expanding the company's presence in international character-based intellectual property development.

75% of Gen Z and Millennials more likely to travel across generations, finds Airbnb survey

Airbnb's 2026 intergenerational travel survey found that 75% of Gen Z and Millennial respondents are more likely to travel with family members across generations. The findings highlight a growing preference for holidays centred on shared experiences, with 55% citing creating memories and 51% strengthening family bonds as key motivations. 

Airbnb reported a more than 55% year-on-year increase in domestic searches for stays by groups of five or more travelling with children or infants. The survey also found that 63% of respondents prioritise relaxing together at their accommodation over sightseeing. Bangalore, Goa, Hyderabad, The Nilgiris and Pondicherry feature among popular domestic destinations.
